opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that you want to be able to actually verify what you find. When you're working with a huge model on some open-ended behavior, it's really easy to tell yourself a nice story — you find a few neurons or a circuit that seem to line up with what you expect, and you convince yourself you've understood the mechanism. But you don't really have ground truth, so you can't tell whether you've explained the whole thing or just a sliver of it.

With small, well-defined tasks, things like subject-verb agreement, indirect object identification, or simple arithmetic, you know exactly what the correct behavior is, and you can design clean counterfactual inputs. So you can do interventions: swap out an activation, patch in a representation from a different input, and check whether the model's behavior changes in exactly the way your hypothesis predicts. That gives you a much tighter feedback loop between hypothesis and evidence.

It's also about building the toolkit. A lot of the methods we use, like causal abstraction, activation patching, and distributed alignment search, were developed and stress-tested on these toy or narrow settings. You need to know your methods work when you can check the answer before you trust them on problems where you can't. In linguistics we sort of did the same thing historically: you study minimal pairs before you try to theorize about all of language.

And finally, I don't think small means trivial. Even simple behaviors in language models often turn out to be implemented in surprisingly complex, distributed, sometimes redundant ways. So you learn real things about how these models organize computation. The hope is that those insights and methods compose, and eventually you can scale up to the messier, more safety-relevant behaviors with a lot more confidence that you're not fooling yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says that open-ended behavior in huge models is hard to assess without ground truth, making it difficult to know whether an explanation is complete. It presents small, well-defined problems as a way to verify findings.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that interpretability is still a field where we don't actually know what the right questions are, let alone the right answers. And when you're in that situation, small problems are where you build intuition.

If you jump straight to "let's understand why a frontier model does X," you're dealing with billions of parameters, behaviors that are tangled up with each other, and no ground truth. You get a result, and you can't tell if it's a real finding or an artifact of your method. So a lot of the work I care about starts with something almost embarrassingly simple, like a toy task where we know exactly what the model needs to compute, or a small model trained on a synthetic distribution. Then you can ask: does my method actually recover the mechanism I know is there? If it doesn't work on that, it's not going to work on GPT-scale models, and you've saved yourself a lot of confusion.

There's also a scientific-method argument. In other fields, you don't start with the most complicated organism. You start with something like a fruit fly or E. coli because you can run controlled experiments quickly and iterate. Interpretability should look more like that. Small problems let you run hundreds of experiments in an afternoon, falsify ideas fast, and build tools that are validated before you point them at something bigger.

And the last piece is that small problems force you to be precise about what "understanding" even means. On a big model you can wave your hands and say "this feature represents sentiment." On a small model, you can actually check whether the thing you found is causally doing what you claim. That discipline, learning what it feels like to have a real explanation versus a story, is what you carry forward when you scale up.

r001.rationale: The candidate says complex frontier models make it hard to distinguish real findings from artifacts, but does not explain that assessing complex reasoning steps is the reason to begin with small problems.

astra-6.text:
I think small problems give you a chance to understand something completely. If you start with a very large model doing a complicated task, you’re trying to figure out both what strategy it’s using and how that strategy is implemented, and there are lots of plausible explanations for any observation.

With a simpler task, you can form a concrete hypothesis and test it. If I think this part of the model is doing a particular computation, can I change it and get the effect I predict? That lets you check whether your explanation actually captures how the model works.

The point isn’t that understanding a small problem automatically solves a bigger one. It’s that you can develop methods and build confidence in them in a setting where you have a better chance of catching your mistakes, and then ask which of those methods carry over.

r001.rationale: The response says that complex tasks in large models make it harder to determine the strategy and its implementation, with many plausible explanations. It presents simpler problems as easier settings for testing explanations and catching mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that with a small problem, you have a chance of knowing whether your explanation is actually right. You can study a model doing a simple task, form a hypothesis about how it works, and then intervene on the model to test that hypothesis. If you think a particular component is doing something, can you change it and get the effect you predicted?

With a much larger model doing a complicated task, it’s easier to come up with a plausible story and much harder to establish that the story captures what’s really happening. So small problems give us a place to develop methods and check our assumptions.

Of course, understanding a small model doesn’t automatically mean we understand a large one. The point is to build reliable tools and then ask which findings carry over as we increase the complexity.

r001.rationale: The response says that with a complicated task it is harder to establish whether an explanation captures what is really happening, and gives that as a reason to start with small problems.
